author: @omsi-fanmark
content:
In Germany, we have quite a lot of supermarkets and discounters offering EV charging and it is the default we (that is my mother and I) use for our two EVs, since most trips are urban and we have to do some shopping anyway. So why not charge during this time? There is a saying in Germany among EV drivers, it translates to: "If it (the car) stands still, it's most likely charging."

Most chargers at such markets are DC fast chargers with rates from 50 kW to 150 kW output (sometimes 150 kW shared between two outlets, so 75 kW each), some also offer AC charging at 11 kW or 22 kW, depending on the vehicle's onboard charger. Sometimes, AC charging is offered even cheaper and is popular among customers who only want to top off their battery a little bit, while customers with low SoC use DC fast charging to have their car full at the end of shopping.

Charging price example:
0,29 EUR / kWh AC
0,44-0,47 EUR / kWh DC (50 kW and below, more than 50 kW)
These are prices from LIDL, others are quite similar. For charging without any monthly basic fee, that is quite reasonable.
